viewBlurbs.cost: Your ticket against everything else you pay — parking, drop-off, food and retail. The gap is what a private operator adds.
viewBlurbs.charges: Each non-ticket charge on its own. Switch them off to see what the total depends on.
viewBlurbs.ticket: The four reported components of a Canadian fare, stacked. Switch any of them off to strip the fare back.
viewBlurbs.revenue: The authorities made no profit on $3.95 billion of 2022 revenue. A private operator has to find 15–20 percent more, every year.
viewBlurbs.books: The 2025 statements of the three busiest airports, from the report's own tables. This is the disclosure a private owner would no longer owe anyone.
viewBlurbs.record: Every measured outcome in the record, with the 2023 study's benefits included rather than buried.

summary.booksLine1: Pearson took in $2.08B in 2025, Montréal-Trudeau $961M, Vancouver $717M — and published every line.
summary.booksLine2: Wages are the largest controllable cost: $297M, $108M and $139M. Rent to Ottawa: $236M, $107M, $78M.
summary.booksLine3: A privately held airport owes the public no such disclosure.
summary.recordLine1: Five countries, three decades: higher charges, pressure on workers, lost public value.
summary.recordLine2: Sydney cut 40% of its workforce once protections expired — the same year it made A$376M profit.
summary.recordLine3: Auckland was found to be earning NZ$190–200M in excess profit; Portugal's charges ran 30% above cost.

article.author: The Data Desk
article.recordLede: The projection rests on what happened elsewhere. The record covers five countries and three decades; one academic study shows genuine benefits alongside the bill.
article.sourcesLede: The reporting carries a footnote block of 15 sources and a closing list of 20. Both are shown.
article.footer: Every paragraph above comes from the reporting; the projections are anchored to its figures and labelled as modelled.
